items.note: States that Udaipur's story is on countless inscriptions.
Describes the single narrow lane of about 300 m from the main road, lined with old stone shops, leading to the temple.
Shops and old house doors are made of stones found in Udaipur itself, with next to no cement or brick: 'Here everything was of stone alone'.
Suggests the town spread over its old plan, with broad orderly roads turning into narrow lanes.
Neelkantheshwar Mahadev temple of the Paramara era is reached by a rear doorway; main east-facing doorway shut for long.
Visitors come to the sanctum for worship and abhisheka, bringing worldly wishes.
Visitors are interested in the deity, few in the architecture or history; photographs taken outside.
Notes stepwells and tanks that no one visits.
Paramara-era constructions and old houses of massive carved stones flank the temple; lanes said to have narrowed by encroachment after the Paramaras.
Paramara kingdom's northern boundary reached Udaipur; Kalachuri territory began beyond; author infers strategic importance of the border town.
Bija Mandal: residential compound whose cellar-like room has a doorway like an old temple's.
At Bija Mandal one side of a door has an eight-line Sanskrit inscription in a square stone frame; the matching panel on the other side is blank.
Ghadiyali family tradition: bells and gongs sounded from this building at fixed times of temple worship; author suggests it was an institution tied to temple activities.
Old temple named Pisanhari; old carved stones reused in lane after lane.
Names Maharaj Udayaditya, who came after King Bhoj, as creator of Udaipur.
Says that after the Paramaras' glory ended Udaipur came into the grip of changes following the Turkish occupation of Delhi; new marks on old constructions.
Ruins of an old palace with rooms and verandas in fair condition and carved stone shelves in the walls.
Author says the palace is not protected by the central government and not among the state's protected monuments.
Between two bastions the twenty-foot stone palace wall was broken for a cement frame and iron gate with a private-property signboard.
Author says no panchayat representative, official, teacher or citizen took initiative for the town's heritage; locals focus on livelihood and farming.
Author and Mishra sketch the layout of Udayaditya's time, with roads cutting at 90 degrees, huge doors and fort-wall watch (their inference).
Describes a broken goddess image on the temple's outer wall, 6.5 to 7 ft up, head struck off, hands cut, with chisel wounds.
Author's general view that between the 9th and 14th centuries dynasties across India built intensively.
Udaipur on the Paramara border touching Kalachuri territory; important because of sandstone quarries; Udayaditya lived there in youth before coronation at Dhara.
Author's post says the settlement of eight thousand still has walls, doorways, temples, palaces, tanks, stepwells and lanes in Paramara architecture on its old design.
Neelkantheshwar temple built by Udayaditya, who came after Bhoj; town's name connected with him.
Author's suggestion that Udayaditya was sent as crown prince to the frontier town and planned its development; settlement must predate him.

claim.value: possibly planned by Udayaditya on a pre-existing settlement (author's inference)

items.note: Stone quarries gave construction material in abundance.
Town not untouched by Islamic invaders; images broken in the temple, yet temple survived in original form.
Visitors come for darshan of the 11th-century temple; few want to study its sculpture.
Author's 2019 letter to the Collector proposing work on the model of the Kashi Vishwanath corridor to place Udaipur on the tourism map.
Reports green cloths recently laid at corners and walls and predicts mazars; author's view of change in the town.
Signboard on the palace wall reads 'Private Property, Udaipur Palace, Ward No. 14, Khasra No. 822' with three Qazi names.
Author says the town was square, encircled by equal walls with a palace within, named after Udayaditya.
Fort wall built on Udaipur's hill in Paramara times, visible even today.
Remains of an unfinished rock-temple project on the Ellora model cut into the hill, with images still visible.
A Jama Masjid board and iron minarets on a building in the lane to the temple will make the mosque more visible than the temple.
Two Arabic or Persian inscriptions on rear doors built from broken temple pieces; Mishra says the name of Mohammad bin Tughlaq was read; dated 1336-1338.
Author describes the goddess image with head severed, ten arms cut off and soles broken, attributing damage to invaders.
Two doors made of temple fragments carry Arabic/Persian inscriptions naming Mohammad bin Tughlaq, 1336-1338, 258 years after Udayaditya, taken as evidence of Tughlaq forces at Udaipur.
Author surmises Udaipur was a last holdout; says last Paramara king Mahlakdeva was killed at Mandu by Ainul Mulk Multani.
Calls this the first named evidence at Udaipur of temple damage; notes Iltutmish 1235 and Alauddin Khilji 1291 attacks on Vidisha, Udaipur spared.
Jain Tirthankara temple said to be smashed; broken Tirthankaras lie among the stones.
Caveat: an inscription alone does not prove Tughlaq did or ordered the damage; earlier raiders may have done it.
Describes the goddess image's cut breasts, broken nose and ears, and disfigured faces.

items.note: Within four days a Tehsildar from Ganj Basoda visited; found nobody living in the self-declared private property on the palace ruins, where a madrasa runs.
Tehsildar says the palace, spread over three-and-a-half bigha, is per revenue records no one's private property.
Claimant says Jahangir laid the foundation stone of the palace, Shah Jahan completed it and gave it to the Qazi family with the qaziyat of 84 villages.
More than twenty inscriptions on the stones of all three doorways of Udayaditya's temple, of the eleventh century.

Udaipur and Patari are rich in stone quarries; the stone is cut, dressed and sent abroad; Ganj Basoda has many businessmen in stone and other trades.

items.note: Jain temple precinct with broken Tirthankara images; author infers Jain followers lived in the town.
Plain Pisanhari temple with matchless carving at its entrance.
Palace niches show Paramara design; stone walls between corridor pillars are later encroachments.
Of eight thousand people, one to one-and-a-half thousand are Muslims; author says their ancestors shaped the town in Udayaditya's time.
Stepwell at the Ghatera Road goddess temple; excavation of a mound found an older stepwell with a 45-degree descent.
Hill has an incomplete Paramara-era rock-temple project with a linga-shaped piece and images being carved; now draped with green cloths.
Huge old stone doorways on lanes and shops filled with rubble suggest the Paramara town's bazaar.
Several 800-900-year-old inscriptions at the sanctum doors, including the name of Udayaditya.
Question of how the temple survived unlike Vidisha's Bija Mandal; suggests local resistance.
